segments.say: So far tonight we've looked at things in space: colours, faces, hands, gorillas. But there is one more thing your brain builds that we almost never question. It's time itself.

You may have heard someone describe a near accident like this. The car skidded, and suddenly everything went into slow motion. I could see the glass, the tree, my own hands on the wheel, all happening so slowly. Maybe it has happened to you. A fall on the stairs, a glass slipping off the table, a bike that wobbles at just the wrong moment.

It's a very common belief. When we're in danger, time itself seems to stretch, as if the brain switches into a high speed mode, taking more snapshots per second, so that we have more time to react. It's a lovely idea. It would be a useful superpower. But is that really what happens?

There are really two ways to explain the slow motion feeling. One is that, in the moment, your brain truly speeds up, like a camera switching to a higher frame rate. The other is that the moment is simply remembered differently, packed with more detail, so that looking back, it feels longer. From the inside, after the fact, these two would feel exactly the same. So how could anyone tell them apart?

show.title: Two possibilities
items: Both would feel the same afterwards
Only a test can tell them apart

segments.say: The neuroscientist David Eagleman had a memory of his own. As a boy, he fell from the roof of a house, and he remembered the fall as strangely slow and long. Years later, he decided to test the feeling properly.

show.title: A scientist with a falling idea

segments.say: In 2007, Chess Stetson, Matthew Fiesta and David Eagleman published a study in the journal PLoS ONE. The question was simple. Does time really slow down during a frightening event? To find out, they needed something truly frightening, but safe.

show.where: Baylor College of Medicine, published 2007 in PLoS ONE
show.what: Volunteers dropped backwards from a tall tower into a net, then judged how long their own fall had taken

segments.say: They chose a ride at an amusement park in Texas, a kind of suspended catch air device. Volunteers were lifted high up, then dropped backwards, in free fall, into a net far below. There were no ropes and no harness to slow them. The fall was about 31 metres, roughly the height of a ten storey building. And it is, by every account, terrifying.

After landing, the volunteers were asked how long their own fall had lasted. Then they watched other people fall the same distance and judged those falls too. On average, people judged their own fall to have lasted about 36 percent longer than the falls they watched. So the feeling was real. Their own fall truly seemed longer.

show.title: Their own fall felt longer
show.label: how much longer people judged their own fall than other people's (Stetson et al., 2007)

segments.say: But that only shows the memory of the fall was long. The real question was whether, during the fall, people actually saw the world faster. If the brain had switched into slow motion, they should be able to take in details that are normally too quick to see.
So the researchers came up with a clever little gadget.

They strapped a small display to each volunteer's wrist. It showed a number, then quickly the same number in reverse colours, switching back and forth. At normal speed, the flicker is just a little too fast for your eye to read the number. It all blurs into an even grey. If time really slowed down during the fall, the volunteers should suddenly be able to read it, the way you can read a spinning wheel in a slow motion film.

show.where: Worn on the wrist during the fall
show.what: A small screen flashed a number and its negative image, too fast to read at normal speed

segments.say: They couldn't. During the fall, people were no better at reading the flickering numbers than they were when they were standing safely on the ground. Their seeing had not sped up at all. What had changed was the memory of the fall afterwards. The brain doesn't run in slow motion during danger. It records more richly, and the recording feels longer when we play it back.

show.title: What they found
items: No one read the fast numbers

segments.say: Why would a frightening moment leave such a long, detailed memory?

One idea is that strong emotion, especially fear, makes the brain lay down memories much more thoroughly. Many parts of the brain involved in emotion, like the amygdala, help strengthen memories of important events. So in those few seconds, the brain stores far more detail than usual. When you remember it later, your brain sees all that detail and concludes that a lot of time must have passed.
Put simply, the brain often judges time by how much it remembers. More memories feel like more time. Fewer memories feel like less.

show.text: More memories feel like more time
show.by: A simple rule your brain seems to follow

segments.say: You may recognise this from everyday life. The first day of a holiday in a new place, full of new streets, new food, new sounds, can feel enormous when you look back. A routine week at home, where every day looks the same, can vanish almost without a trace. While it's happening, a boring hour drags. But afterwards, the exciting days are the ones that seem long.

So your sense of how long something took is not a reading from a clock inside your head. It's a reconstruction, built afterwards, from what you stored. Like the colours, the edges and the hands we met earlier, time is something your brain assembles.

If more memories make time feel longer, that suggests a gentle little idea for everyday life. When the weeks seem to slip away too fast, you can give your memory more to hold. Visit somewhere new, even a nearby park you've never walked through. Take a different route home. Notice small details, the colour of a door, the smell of rain. Or write a single line each evening about what was different today. None of this changes the clock. But it may change how full your days feel when you look back on them.

show.title: Ways to make time feel fuller
items: Write a line about your day

segments.say: Many people also feel that the years go faster as they get older. Psychologists have offered several possible explanations, and no one is completely sure. But one idea fits neatly with what we've just seen. Childhood is full of firsts, and firsts leave rich memories. Later on, when more days follow familiar patterns, there may simply be fewer new memories to fill the years, so looking back, they seem shorter.

show.cap: Why years seem to speed up

segments.say: Let's set the belief and the evidence side by side.

The belief says danger switches the brain into slow motion, so that you see more in the moment. The science says your perception keeps its normal speed, and what changes is the memory. You don't see more. You remember more, and memory is what makes the moment feel long.

show.title: Time in danger
items: Belief: danger switches on slow motion
Science: perception stays the same speed
Belief: you see more in the moment

segments.say: As always, it's worth keeping a little humility. This was one study, with a small number of brave volunteers, and one kind of fear, a short fall. Other kinds of danger might work differently, and scientists are still studying how the brain keeps track of time. But it's a beautiful example of how a feeling we're all sure about can turn out to be a story the brain tells afterwards.

show.sub: One study, one kind of fear

segments.say: And that leads us toward our last belief of the night, perhaps the biggest of all. If your brain builds colour, sound, touch, pain and even time, then a natural question follows. Is the world your brain builds the same as the one built by the person next to you?

show.sub: Not everyone's world is the same
